# Overview

In Autumn 2026, every Psych 251 student replicates a published experiment (Phase 1) and then runs
a second version of it (Phase 2). On the default track, Phase 2 is a **best-practices
modification**: one to three changes drawn from Experimentology (measurement, design, sample,
instructions and checks, analysis), with everything else held constant. Students who opt in to the
metascience project receive additional participant budget, have their projects analysed here, and
are authors on the resulting paper.

A Phase 2 is informally a "rescue" when Phase 1 failed and an "upgrade" when it succeeded. **We
treat these as one category and never compare them**: the changes come from the same menu, and any
contrast between them is confounded with regression to the mean, because projects are sorted into
the two groups by their Phase 1 result (see [Sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity)).

We ask whether these extensions change what a replication finds.

- **RQ1, replication success.** Across all projects, is Phase 2 judged a successful replication of
  the original more often than Phase 1?
- **RQ2, effect size.** Across all projects, does the Phase 2 estimate, expressed as a ratio to the
  original effect, differ from the Phase 1 estimate? This is a question about estimation, not about
  saving effects. Better measurement can raise a standardized effect by reducing measurement error,
  but if the true effect is small, a precise Phase 2 that finds a small effect is a good outcome.
- **RQ3, precision.** Across all projects, how much smaller is the Phase 2 standard error than
  Phase 1's, beyond what the change in sample size alone predicts?
- Only RQ1 uses the language of replication "success", which means agreement with the original
  finding, as in Boyce et al. (2023, 2024).
- **Context.** How do the 2026 results compare with the 17 rescues in Boyce et al. (2024)? This is
  descriptive only (see [Comparison with Boyce et al. (2024)](#comparison-boyce)).

# Background

- **Boyce, Mathur & Frank (2023).** 176 Psych 251 replications over 11 years; mean subjective
  replication score 49%; 76/176 (43%) scored mostly or fully replicated (≥ .75).
- **Boyce et al. (2024).** 17 "rescues" of failed class replications, run by a different student in
  a later year. 5/17 (29%, bootstrapped 95% CI 12%–53%) mostly or fully replicated; every rescue
  estimate was smaller than the original. The largest (post hoc) correlates of rescue success were
  a small first-replication sample and a large rescue-to-first-replication sample ratio (both
  *r* = .49). Outcomes, rating procedure and effect-size conversions are in
  `langcog/251-rescue-projects`; we reuse them here wherever possible.

What is different in 2026:

| | Boyce et al. (2024) | This project |
|---|---|---|
| Who runs the second study | A different student, one or more years later | The same student, about two weeks later |
| Which projects | Failed replications only (score ≤ .5) | All opted-in Track 1 projects, whether or not Phase 1 succeeded |
| Changes allowed | Fix plausible causes of failure | 1–3 tagged best-practices changes, everything else identical |
| Implementation | Student-built | Agent-assisted, from a common template (jsPsych + Firebase) |
| Budget | Class budget | Additional budget for opted-in projects |

# Design

## Projects

- **Population.** Students enrolled in Psych 251, Autumn 2026, who opt in to the metascience
  project. Opting in is what makes a project part of this study; projects that are not opted in are
  ordinary course projects and are not analysed.
- **Track 2 (scientific extension) projects are excluded entirely**, whether or not the student
  opted in.
- **Project-level exclusions [D1].** A project is excluded if Phase 2 was not run, or if the key
  statistic cannot be computed for the original, Phase 1 or Phase 2. Every excluded project is
  listed with its reason.
- **Expected number.** About 20 students are enrolled; we expect most to opt in, so *k* ≈ 15–20.
  The sensitivity analysis below covers *k* = 10–30.

## Selection on the Phase 1 result

The pooled comparison of Phase 2 with Phase 1 is unbiased only if *which projects are included*
does not depend on how Phase 1 came out (see [RQ2](#rq2)). Two features of the course can violate
this, and we record what is needed to check and correct for them:

- **Track 2 requires a successful replication**, so excluding Track 2 removes some projects with high
  Phase 1 estimates. We report how many Track 2 projects there were and their Phase 1 scores.
- **Opting in may happen after a student has seen their Phase 1 result.** We record the date each
  student opted in, and whether it was before or after their Phase 1 data were in.
- Projects excluded under D1 are reported with their Phase 1 scores.

# Measures

## Subjective replication score (RQ1)

- Scale and procedure from Boyce et al. (2024): each phase is rated on 0 / .25 / .5 / .75 / 1 for
  how well it replicates the original on the key result, considering direction, magnitude and
  significance together rather than any single cutoff. **Success = ≥ .75** ("mostly" or "fully").
- **Rubric and calibration.** Raters use the written anchors for each scale point from Boyce et al.
  (2023) *[to add: anchor text from V. Boyce]*, with one worked example per level drawn from past
  class projects. Before rating Phase 1, all four raters independently rate 2–3 past projects from
  the Boyce et al. (2023) sample and compare their ratings with the published scores.
- **Raters.** All four course staff (MCF and the three TAs) rate every project independently. A
  project's score for a phase is the mean of the four ratings. We report inter-rater agreement
  (intraclass correlation, and the Spearman correlation of each pair as in Boyce et al., 2024) and
  list projects where ratings span more than .25.
- **When, and from what.** Phase 1 is rated during the midterm presentations (November 4 and 6),
  from the slides, which show the original and the replication side by side. A project without
  Phase 1 data by then is rated from its report as soon as the data are in, and always before any
  Phase 2 data exist. Phase 2 is rated during the final presentations, or from the final report if
  the data were not in by then. Ratings are entered independently, before any discussion of the
  project among the raters.
- Student self-ratings (if collected) are reported separately and are not an outcome.

## Key effect and its extraction

- **Key effect.** The single key analysis of interest in the student's Phase 1 preregistration.
  Phase 2 uses the same key analysis unless the Changes table lists an Analysis change; in that case
  the effect is computed both ways where possible, and the preregistered Phase 1 version is primary.
- **Extraction by re-running the student's pipeline.** For Phase 1 and Phase 2 we re-run the
  analysis in the student's report from the anonymized data committed to their repository
  (`data/raw/<experiment id>/`), with agent assistance and human verification, and take the key
  test statistic from that run. We also record the value the student reported. A mismatch is
  recorded and resolved, and the rate of mismatches is reported as a by-product: it is a
  computational reproducibility check of the class reports (see agent reproducibility audits,
  below).
- **Original effect.** From the original paper, as coded by the student in the report's
  `original-study` chunk, checked by a second person.

## Effect sizes

- **Metric.** Standardized mean difference (SMD), using the conversions in
  `langcog/251-rescue-projects/code/helper/parse_stats.R` so that the numbers are comparable with
  Boyce et al. (2023, 2024), with Hedges' small-sample correction. Signs are aligned so that the
  original effect is positive and an effect in the opposite direction is negative.
- **Standardizer caveat [D5].** Those conversions give *d* for between-participant tests and
  *d*<sub>z</sub> for within-participant tests. A Phase 2 that changes the design (for example
  between → within) therefore changes the standardizer as well as the estimate. Proposed: in that
  case also compute Phase 2 with the Phase 1 standardizer where the data allow, use that as primary,
  and flag the project.
- **Effect size ratio (primary for RQ2).** For each phase, *r* = SMD<sub>phase</sub> /
  SMD<sub>original</sub>. *r* = 1 means the original effect size was recovered; *r* = 0 means no
  effect; *r* < 0 means the opposite direction.
- **Precision (RQ3).** SE ratio = SE<sub>Phase 2</sub> / SE<sub>Phase 1</sub> of the SMD,
  compared with the ratio expected from sample size alone, √(*N*<sub>1</sub>/*N*<sub>2</sub>). The
  part of the precision gain not explained by *N* is attributable to the other changes.
- **Statistical consistency (secondary, as in Boyce et al. 2024).** *p*-original (Mathur &
  VanderWeele, 2020) with imputed heterogeneity τ = .21 SMD, for original vs Phase 1, original vs
  Phase 2, and original vs both phases combined.

## Project covariates

- The Boyce et al. (2023, 2024) set: subfield, within/between design, single vignette, number of
  trials, open data, open materials, switch to online, original and replication sample sizes.
- The Phase 2 change categories from each report's Changes table (Measurement, Trials, Design,
  Checks, Instructions, Sample, Analysis), and the Phase 2 / Phase 1 sample-size ratio.
- Exploratory covariates in [Exploratory analyses](#exploratory).

# Analysis plan

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (runs on simulated data until real data exist)"

# DerSimonian-Laird random-effects estimate of the mean and between-project variance.
dl_meta <- function(y, se) {
  w     <- 1 / se^2
  mu_fe <- sum(w * y) / sum(w)
  q     <- sum(w * (y - mu_fe)^2)
  tau2  <- max(0, (q - (length(y) - 1)) / (sum(w) - sum(w^2) / sum(w)))
  w_re  <- 1 / (se^2 + tau2)
  list(mu = sum(w_re * y) / sum(w_re), tau2 = tau2)
}

# Expected Phase 2 SMD if Phase 2 changed nothing: the Phase 1 estimate shrunk toward the class
# mean in proportion to its noise (empirical Bayes). Because it conditions on the Phase 1
# estimate, comparing Phase 2 with this prediction stays valid when inclusion depends on Phase 1.
eb_predict <- function(d1, se1) {
  m <- dl_meta(d1, se1)
  m$mu + m$tau2 / (m$tau2 + se1^2) * (d1 - m$mu)
}

boot_prop_ci <- function(x, B = 2000) {
  if (length(x) == 0) return(c(NA_real_, NA_real_))
  quantile(replicate(B, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE))), c(.025, .975), names = FALSE)
}

mean_ci <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  if (length(x) < 2) return(tibble(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), low = NA_real_, high = NA_real_))
  tt <- t.test(x)
  tibble(n = length(x), mean = mean(x), low = tt$conf.int[1], high = tt$conf.int[2])
}

# One row per project: d_orig, d1, se1, n1, d2, se2, n2, score1, score2 (mean staff ratings).
add_ratios <- function(proj) {
  proj |>
    mutate(r1 = d1 / d_orig, r2 = d2 / d_orig,
           change = r2 - r1,
           change_eb = (d2 - eb_predict(d1, se1)) / d_orig,
           se_ratio = se2 / se1,
           se_ratio_from_n = sqrt(n1 / n2))
}

fmt_rate <- function(x) {
  ci <- boot_prop_ci(x)
  tibble(Successes = sprintf("%d of %d", sum(x), length(x)),
         Rate = scales::percent(mean(x), accuracy = 1),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.0f%%, %.0f%%]", 100 * ci[1], 100 * ci[2]))
}

# RQ1: success rates for each phase across all projects, and the paired Phase 1 x Phase 2 table.
success_table <- function(proj) {
  bind_rows(
    fmt_rate(proj$score1 >= .75) |> mutate(Phase = "Phase 1", `Mean score` = sprintf("%.2f", mean(proj$score1))),
    fmt_rate(proj$score2 >= .75) |> mutate(Phase = "Phase 2", `Mean score` = sprintf("%.2f", mean(proj$score2)))
  ) |>
    relocate(Phase)
}

# RQ2: change in effect size ratio (Phase 2 minus Phase 1), pooled over all projects. The raw
# change is confirmatory; the change beyond the empirical-Bayes prediction is the robustness check.
# Inverse-variance-weighted (random-effects) pooled change, so that noisy projects count for less.
# The sampling variance of r2 - r1 treats the original SMD as fixed.
weighted_change <- function(proj) {
  se_change <- sqrt(proj$se1^2 + proj$se2^2) / abs(proj$d_orig)
  m  <- dl_meta(proj$change, se_change)
  se <- sqrt(1 / sum(1 / (se_change^2 + m$tau2)))
  tibble(n = nrow(proj), mean = m$mu, low = m$mu - 1.96 * se, high = m$mu + 1.96 * se)
}

ratio_table <- function(proj) {
  bind_rows(
    mean_ci(proj$change)    |> mutate(Estimate = "Change in ratio (confirmatory)"),
    mean_ci(proj$change_eb) |> mutate(Estimate = "Change beyond regression to the mean (robustness)"),
    weighted_change(proj)   |> mutate(Estimate = "Inverse-variance-weighted change (robustness)")
  ) |>
    transmute(Estimate, k = n, Mean = sprintf("%.2f", mean),
              `95% CI` = if_else(is.na(low), "", sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", low, high)))
}

ratio_plot <- function(proj) {
  proj |>
    select(project, `Phase 1` = r1, `Phase 2` = r2) |>
    pivot_longer(c(`Phase 1`, `Phase 2`), names_to = "Phase", values_to = "ratio") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = Phase, y = ratio, group = project)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
    geom_point(aes(colour = Phase), size = 2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1E6E76", "#B8792A"), guide = "none") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Effect size ratio (replication SMD / original SMD)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}
```

## RQ1: replication success

- **Primary estimate.** The proportion of projects whose Phase 2 is a success (mean staff score
  ≥ .75), next to the same proportion for Phase 1, each with a bootstrapped 95% CI, and the paired
  Phase 1 × Phase 2 cross-tabulation. Also reported: mean scores, and the statistical criterion
  (key test significant at α = .05 in the original direction) for each phase.
- No hypothesis test: with *k* ≈ 15–20 the intervals will be wide, and the estimate is reported as
  such.
- **Descriptive only:** among projects whose Phase 1 failed, the proportion whose Phase 2
  succeeded. This conditional rate is affected by regression to the mean, and is reported only
  because it is the quantity Boyce et al. (2024) reported, whose rescues were selected the same way
  (see [Comparison with Boyce et al. (2024)](#comparison-boyce)).

## RQ2: effect size ratio {#rq2}

- **Primary estimate and test.** The mean, across all included projects, of the change in effect
  size ratio, *r*<sub>2</sub> − *r*<sub>1</sub>, with a 95% CI. Prediction: the mean change is
  greater than 0, because better measurement reduces the attenuation of standardized effects
  (one-sided *t* test, α = .05) **[D6]**. Given the expected number of
  projects, this is primarily an estimate with a wide interval (see
  [Sensitivity analysis](#sensitivity)).
- **Why pooled.** If Phase 2 changed nothing, the Phase 1 and Phase 2 estimates would both be
  unbiased estimates of the same true effect, so their difference would average zero for every
  project, whatever its true effect. Pooling over all projects is therefore unbiased **provided
  inclusion does not depend on the Phase 1 result**. Any subgroup defined by the Phase 1 result
  (such as rescues or upgrades) is biased by regression to the mean: projects selected for a low
  Phase 1 estimate rise on average, and those selected for a high one fall.
- **Robustness to selection on Phase 1.** Excluding Track 2 projects, and opting in after seeing
  Phase 1, can make inclusion depend on the Phase 1 result (see
  [Selection on the Phase 1 result](#selection-on-the-phase-1-result)). As a robustness check we
  report the pooled change relative to an empirical-Bayes prediction of Phase 2 from Phase 1 (the
  Phase 1 estimate shrunk toward the class mean in proportion to its standard error). Because it
  conditions on the Phase 1 estimate, it remains approximately unbiased under such selection. If
  the two estimates differ materially, we report both and say so.
- **Interpretation.** Changes that make measurement more reliable are expected to *increase* the
  standardized effect, because measurement error inflates the standardizer. Changes to sample size
  alone are not: they change precision, not the expected effect. The change-category analysis
  below (exploratory) looks at this directly. A Phase 2 whose ratio stays low with a narrow
  interval is evidence that the true effect is small, and we will describe it that way, not as a
  failed rescue.
- **Sample size and noise.** A smaller sample makes an estimate noisier, not larger on average:
  small samples inflate effects only when results are filtered on significance, and every included
  project is analysed whatever its result. We report the Phase 2 / Phase 1 sample-size ratio, use
  Hedges' correction, and add an inverse-variance-weighted pooled change as a robustness check, so
  that noisy projects count for less. (Sample size does affect RQ1, because the subjective score
  takes significance into account.)
- **Robustness to small originals.** Ratios are unstable when the original SMD is small. We report
  the median change and a version excluding projects with |SMD<sub>original</sub>| < .2 **[D7]**,
  and the same analysis on the SMD scale (*d*<sub>2</sub> − *d*<sub>1</sub>, random-effects
  meta-analysis).

## RQ3: precision

- **Primary estimate.** The mean, across projects, of the log SE ratio (Phase 2 / Phase 1) minus
  the log of the ratio expected from sample size alone, √(*N*<sub>1</sub>/*N*<sub>2</sub>), with a
  95% CI: the precision gain from changes other than *N*. Values below 0 mean Phase 2 was more
  precise than its sample size alone would predict.
- Also reported: the observed SE ratio and the ratio expected from *N*, each as a geometric mean.
  The observed ratio mostly reflects sample size, so it is descriptive only.

## Comparison with Boyce et al. (2024) {#comparison-boyce}

- **Registered as descriptive only: no quantitative comparison is possible.** The samples differ in
  who ran the second study, how long after the first replication, what changes were allowed, the
  budget, and the tools, and both samples are small and self-selected. We show the 2026 conditional
  rate (Phase 2 success among Phase 1 failures) and effect size ratios next to the 2024 values in
  one table and one figure, and discuss differences qualitatively.

```{r}
#| label: boyce-2024
boyce_2024 <- tibble(
  Study = "Boyce et al. (2024) rescues",
  Projects = 17,
  `Mostly or fully replicated (≥ .75)` = "5 (29%)",
  `95% CI` = "[12%, 53%]",
  Source = "Results, 'Overall replication rate'"

knitr::kable(boyce_2024, caption = "Reference values from Boyce et al. (2024). The 2026 row is added when data exist.")
```

## Exploratory analyses {#exploratory}

All exploratory and labelled as such; *k* is too small for confirmatory moderator tests.

1. **Change category.** RQ1 and RQ2 outcomes by the categories in each project's Changes table
   (projects can have more than one), and by the Phase 2 / Phase 1 sample-size ratio, the strongest
   correlate in Boyce et al. (2024).
2. **Textual ambiguity of the original procedure** as a covariate of Phase 1 and Phase 2 success
   and of the effect size ratio **[D8]**. Candidate measures: (a) the number of rows in the
   report's "Differences from the original study" table plus the choices listed in its Analysis
   plan as not specified by the original; (b) an agent-coded count of procedural details a
   replicator would need but the original Methods does not give, checked by a human coder on a
   subset. Open: how systematic the rating should be, and what coding system to use.
3. **Agent reproducibility audits** **[D9]**. (a) Original papers: an agent checks each original
   paper's reported statistics for internal consistency (test statistic, df and *p*;
   GRIM/GRIMMER-style checks of means and SDs where *N* is known) and lists flagged issues, which a
   person verifies. Outcome: the number of verified issues per paper, reported descriptively and as a
   covariate of replication success. (b) Student pipelines: the re-run described under
   [Key effect and its extraction](#key-effect-and-its-extraction); outcome: the rate of mismatches
   between re-run and reported key statistics. Open: when the audits happen, and who runs and
   verifies them.
4. The Boyce et al. (2023, 2024) project covariates, as correlations with Phase 1 and Phase 2
   scores.

## Possible second aim: reproducibility with and without a researcher **[D14]**

Problem Set 3 (due November 22) has two students per paper reproduce a recent open-data article
with an agent under their direction, within 4 hours, and give a verdict on each target outcome.
Running a fully automated agent on the same papers, with no student involved, would compare
researcher-directed with fully automated reproducibility on the same corpus.

- The automated runs use a fixed prompt and model, are specified before November 22, and are
  completed and frozen before anyone looks at the student verdicts.
- Outcome: agreement between the automated and student verdicts on each target outcome, and the
  proportion of outcomes each reproduced.
- The paper-level verdicts are about the papers. Student transcripts and time accounting are data
  about students, so analysing them falls under the same new IRB protocol as the measures below.
- This addresses a different question from RQ1–3, so it may fit better as a companion paper.

## Measures that need a separate protocol (not part of this registration)

Each of these makes students, not their experiments, the object of study. Each needs a new IRB
protocol and sign-off from the Stanford student research committee before anything is collected,
and participation must not affect grades. They are listed here so the plan is complete; none will be
collected under this registration **[D10]**.

| Measure | Idea | Main concerns |
|---|---|---|
| AI attitudes survey | Post-quarter survey of attitudes toward AI agents in research | No pre-measure is possible now; consent separate from course |
| AI chat logs | Analyse students' agent transcripts from the project | Uneven export across tools; logs can contain participant data or keys; consent and anonymization |
| Comprehension quiz | Low-stakes quiz generated from each student's own repository, testing whether they understand what they did | Must be ungraded or very low stakes; question validity; consent |

# Sensitivity analysis {#sensitivity}

How informative is RQ2 with the number of projects we expect, how large is the
regression-to-the-mean bias in subgroups defined by Phase 1, and how much does selection on Phase 1
bias the pooled estimate? We simulate classes of *k* projects. Original SMDs are drawn from
0.3–1.0; each project's true Phase 1 effect is the original times a factor drawn from
N(0.5, 0.35), so replications recover about half the original effect on average, with
heterogeneity; Phase 1 total *N* is 40–150. A project's Phase 1 counts as a success if its estimate
is significant in the original direction (a stand-in for the subjective score). Phase 2 has a
standard error 1/1.4 of Phase 1's, and its true effect is the Phase 1 true effect times (1 + *g*),
where *g* is the proportional gain in the true effect from better methods. With replications
recovering about half the original effect, *g* = 0.3 moves the expected effect size ratio from about
0.50 to 0.65. To mimic the Track 2 exclusion, a selection scenario drops each project with a
successful Phase 1 with probability .3.

```{r}
#| label: simulation
sim_once <- function(k, gain, precision_gain = 1.4, p_drop_success = 0.3) {
  d_orig  <- runif(k, 0.3, 1.0)
  delta   <- d_orig * rnorm(k, 0.5, 0.35)
  n1      <- sample(40:150, k, replace = TRUE)
  se1     <- 2 / sqrt(n1)
  d1      <- rnorm(k, delta, se1)
  success <- d1 / se1 >= qnorm(0.975)
  d2      <- rnorm(k, delta * (1 + gain), se1 / precision_gain)
  naive     <- (d2 - d1) / d_orig
  corrected <- (d2 - eb_predict(d1, se1)) / d_orig
  # Selection scenario: some Phase 1 successes leave the sample (as Track 2 projects do).
  kept <- !(success & runif(k) < p_drop_success)
  corrected_kept <- (d2[kept] - eb_predict(d1[kept], se1[kept])) / d_orig[kept]
  c(pooled                 = mean(naive),
    failed_naive           = mean(naive[!success]),
    succeeded_naive        = mean(naive[success]),
    failed_corrected       = mean(corrected[!success]),
    succeeded_corrected    = mean(corrected[success]),
    selected_naive         = mean(naive[kept]),
    selected_corrected     = mean(corrected_kept),
    reject                 = t.test(naive, alternative = "greater")$p.value < .05)
}

sims <- expand_grid(k = c(10, 20, 30), gain = c(0, 0.15, 0.3), rep = 1:1000) |>
  mutate(out = map2(k, gain, ~ as_tibble_row(sim_once(.x, .y)))) |>
  unnest(out)
```

```{r}
#| label: sim-power
sims |>
  group_by(k, gain) |>
  summarise(`P(reject), pooled test` = scales::percent(mean(reject), accuracy = 1),
            `SD of pooled estimate` = sprintf("%.2f", sd(pooled)), .groups = "drop") |>
  rename(`Projects (k)` = k, `True proportional gain (g)` = gain) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Rejection rate of the pooled one-sided test of RQ2 (false-positive rate when g = 0, power otherwise), from 1,000 simulated classes per cell.")

sim_summary <- sims |>
  group_by(k, gain) |>
  summarise(power = mean(reject), sd = sd(pooled),
            across(c(pooled, failed_naive, succeeded_naive, failed_corrected,
                     succeeded_corrected, selected_naive, selected_corrected),
                   ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
            .groups = "drop")
s20  <- filter(sim_summary, k == 20, gain == 0.3)
s20n <- filter(sim_summary, k == 20, gain == 0)
```

**What this means.** With 20 projects, the pooled test has
`r scales::percent(s20$power, accuracy = 1)` power to detect a Phase 2 true effect 30% larger than
Phase 1's (*g* = 0.3: for example, recovering 65% of the original effect instead of 50%, a change of
about 0.15 in the ratio), and the 95% CI on the pooled change will be roughly
±`r sprintf("%.2f", 1.96 * s20$sd)`. RQ2 is therefore best read as an estimate with a wide interval
rather than a decisive test, and the registration should say so.

When Phase 2 changes nothing (*g* = 0, *k* = 20), the pooled raw change averages
`r sprintf("%+.2f", s20n$pooled)`. Split by the Phase 1 result, it averages
`r sprintf("%+.2f", s20n$failed_naive)` for projects whose Phase 1 failed and
`r sprintf("%+.2f", s20n$succeeded_naive)` for those whose Phase 1 succeeded, from selection alone,
which is why we never compare those groups. When Phase 1 successes are partly removed from the
sample, as the Track 2 exclusion does, the pooled raw change averages
`r sprintf("%+.2f", s20n$selected_naive)` and the empirically corrected change
`r sprintf("%+.2f", s20n$selected_corrected)`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bias
sim_summary |>
  filter(gain == 0) |>
  transmute(`Projects (k)` = k,
            `All projects` = sprintf("%+.3f", pooled),
            `Phase 1 failed` = sprintf("%+.3f", failed_naive),
            `Phase 1 succeeded` = sprintf("%+.3f", succeeded_naive),
            `Successes partly excluded: raw` = sprintf("%+.3f", selected_naive),
            `Successes partly excluded: corrected` = sprintf("%+.3f", selected_corrected)) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Mean estimated change in effect size ratio when Phase 2 changes nothing (g = 0). Any value away from zero is bias.")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rtm
#| fig-cap: "Estimated change in effect size ratio in simulated classes of 20 projects where Phase 2 changes nothing (g = 0), split by the Phase 1 result. The raw change is biased upward when Phase 1 failed and downward when it succeeded, by selection alone; the change beyond the empirical-Bayes prediction is close to zero for both. This is why rescues and upgrades are never compared."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5
sims |>
  filter(k == 20, gain == 0) |>
  select(failed_naive, succeeded_naive, failed_corrected, succeeded_corrected) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("type", "estimate"), names_sep = "_") |>
  mutate(type = if_else(type == "failed", "Phase 1 failed", "Phase 1 succeeded"),
         estimate = factor(estimate, c("naive", "corrected"),
                           c("Raw change", "Change beyond regression to the mean"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = estimate)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, colour = NA, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ type) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey55", "#1E6E76")) +
  labs(x = "Mean change in effect size ratio (Phase 2 − Phase 1)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

# Results

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| include: false
# Real data: one row per project, built from data/extracted/effects.csv and data/ratings.csv once
# extraction is done. Until then the results below run on one simulated class and say so.
projects_path <- file.path("..", "data", "extracted", "projects.csv")
have_data <- file.exists(projects_path)

if (have_data) {
  proj <- read_csv(projects_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |> add_ratios()
} else {
  k <- 18
  d_orig <- runif(k, 0.3, 1.0); delta <- d_orig * rnorm(k, 0.5, 0.35)
  n1 <- sample(40:150, k, TRUE); n2 <- round(n1 * runif(k, 1, 2.5))
  se1 <- 2 / sqrt(n1); se2 <- 2 / sqrt(n2)
  d1 <- rnorm(k, delta, se1); d2 <- rnorm(k, delta * 1.15, se2)
  rate <- function(d, se) case_when(d / se > 2.5 ~ 1, d / se > 1.96 ~ .75, d > 0 ~ .25, TRUE ~ 0)
  proj <- tibble(project = sprintf("sim%02d", 1:k), d_orig, d1, se1, n1, d2, se2, n2,
                 score1 = rate(d1, se1), score2 = rate(d2, se2)) |>
    add_ratios()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: data-notice
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!have_data) {
  cat("::: {.callout-warning icon=false}\n",
      "## Simulated data\n\n",
      "No extracted project data yet (`data/extracted/projects.csv`). **Everything in this section ",
      "is computed from one simulated class of ", nrow(proj), " projects** to check that the ",
      "analysis code runs end to end. None of these numbers are results.\n",
      ":::\n", sep = "")
}
```

## RQ1: replication success

```{r}
#| label: rq1
success_table(proj) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Replication success (mean staff score ≥ .75) in each phase, all projects.")

table(`Phase 1` = if_else(proj$score1 >= .75, "Success", "Failure"),
      `Phase 2` = if_else(proj$score2 >= .75, "Success", "Failure")) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 1 by Phase 2 success (rows: Phase 1).")
```

## RQ2: effect size ratio

```{r}
#| label: rq2
ratio_table(proj) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Change in effect size ratio, Phase 2 minus Phase 1, pooled over all projects.")

pooled_test <- t.test(proj$change, alternative = "greater")
```

Pooled one-sided test: *t*(`r pooled_test$parameter`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", pooled_test$statistic)`,
*p* = `r format.pval(pooled_test$p.value, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ratios
#| fig-cap: "Effect size ratio (replication SMD / original SMD) for Phase 1 and Phase 2 of each project. The dashed line is the original effect size; the solid line is no effect."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
ratio_plot(proj)
```

## RQ3: precision

```{r}
#| label: precision
gain_beyond_n <- mean_ci(log(proj$se_ratio) - log(proj$se_ratio_from_n))
proj |>
  summarise(Projects = n(),
            `Observed SE ratio (geometric mean)` = sprintf("%.2f", exp(mean(log(se_ratio)))),
            `Expected from N alone` = sprintf("%.2f", exp(mean(log(se_ratio_from_n)))),
            `Beyond N (ratio, 95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", exp(gain_beyond_n$mean),
                                                 exp(gain_beyond_n$low), exp(gain_beyond_n$high))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2 / Phase 1 standard error of the key SMD.")
```

# Data and code

- `data/extracted/effects.csv`: one row per project × study (original, Phase 1, Phase 2): project
  repository, test description, raw test statistic, *N*, within/between, same direction, source
  (pipeline re-run or reported), SMD, SE.
- `data/ratings.csv`: one row per project × phase × rater (four raters): score, date, materials
  rated (presentation or report).
- `data/extracted/projects.csv`: one row per included project, built from the two files above.
- Opt-in dates and Track 2 status are recorded privately (see
  [Selection on the Phase 1 result](#selection-on-the-phase-1-result)) and reported in aggregate.
- Student repositories are public under the psych251 GitHub organization. Which students opted in
  is recorded privately until the author list is public **[D11]**.

# Decision points {#decision-points}

| | Decision | Options | Proposed or decided | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | Project-level exclusions | As above; also exclude if Phase 2 deviates from its preregistration in a way that changes the key test? | As above, plus list and justify any others before unblinding | Open |
| D2 | Rescue vs upgrade | Classify and compare; treat as one category | One category, never compared; conditional rate reported descriptively for the Boyce et al. (2024) comparison only | **Decided Nov 2** |
| D3 | When and from what staff rate each phase | Both at final presentations; each phase as its data come in | Phase 1 at the midterms, or from the report if data were not in; Phase 2 at the finals, or from the final report; Phase 1 always before Phase 2 data exist | **Decided Nov 2** |
| D4 | Raters | Two TAs; two TAs excluding the project's own; MCF + one TA as in 2024; all four staff | All four staff rate every project; score is the mean | **Decided Nov 2** |
| D5 | Standardizer when Phase 2 changes design | Use the conversion as is; recompute with the Phase 1 standardizer | Recompute where data allow; flag | Open |
| D6 | RQ2 confirmatory test | One-sided pooled *t* test; estimation only; Bayesian | One-sided pooled *t* test plus estimate and CI; empirical-Bayes-corrected change as robustness check | Open |
| D7 | Guard against small original SMDs | None; exclude |SMD| < .2 as a robustness check; use the difference scale | Robustness check only | Open |
| D8 | Ambiguity ratings | Count from report tables; agent-coded with human check; both. How systematic, what coding system | Both, (a) primary | Open |
| D9 | Agent reproducibility audits | When (before or after Phase 2 data), who runs them, who verifies (TA or student), whether students see results before Phase 2 | Run after Phase 2 data are in; TA verifies | Open |
| D10 | Attitudes, chat logs, comprehension quiz | Pursue some under a new protocol; drop for 2026 | Decide after checking IRB and student research committee timelines | Open: needs new IRB |
| D11 | Public roster of opted-in projects | Public now; private until the author list is public | Private until the paper | Open |
| D12 | Phase 2 deadline and late projects | Include all projects with Phase 2 data by Nov 30; later | Nov 30 (the M5 data deadline) | Open |
| D14 | PS3 reproducibility as a second aim | Leave out; add as a second aim here; companion paper | Add a fully automated baseline, frozen before student verdicts are read; decide where it is reported | Open, **needs specifying by Nov 22** |
| D13 | Scope: one year or a cumulative series | Report 2026 alone; register 2026 as wave 1 of a series that pools future years with the same two-phase design | Report 2026 now and register it as wave 1; earlier years are not pooled because the design is new | Open |
